summary:
A pixel-art card game for all age groups. 

Cadets run Moon Base Shackleton, near the Moon’s south pole, for 10 days. Their guide is Tar-Ra, a hologram named after Terra (Latin for Earth), who welcomes them as new cadets and teaches them through a tutorial.

Each day, players draw three cards and choose one. Every card has a benefit and a cost, such as splitting water to make oxygen at the price of power. Players must keep Power and Air above zero, build Shield against radiation, and collect Science.

Solar storm risk comes from real NASA DONKI space-weather data. The game says clearly whether that data is live or a dated saved reading. Each card teaches a real fact drawn from NASA research. At the end, Tar-Ra scores the mission and gives a personal tip.

This answers the challenge by turning life support, radiation shielding and power into choices kids actually make, where no option is free. That is the thinking real mission planners use. 

Tar-Ra matters because tomorrow’s explorers learn best by doing. 

Kids leave understanding why living beyond Earth is hard, and why careful planning keeps astronauts alive.

The game is playable in English and Montenegrin!
details:
What it does and how it works

Tar-Ra’s Moon Mission Trainer is a pixel-art strategy card game targeted for youth. Players are new cadets running Moon Base Shackleton, near the Moon’s south pole, for 10 days.

The guide. Tar-Ra is a calm, wise hologram named after Terra, the Latin word for Earth. She runs a short tutorial. It introduces the four things the base needs, makes each one glow on screen as she explains it, and lets kids play a practice card before the real mission starts.

Each day:

  • Morning: sunlight recharges the solar panels.
  • Choice: the player draws 3 cards from a shuffled deck and plays 1. All 16 card types have a benefit (HELPS) and a cost (COSTS). For example, splitting water makes oxygen but uses a lot of power.
  • Night: the base uses up Power, Air and some Shield.
  • Storms: Tar-Ra warns a day ahead. If Shield is too low when the storm hits, the crew loses a day hiding and uses extra air.
  • Failure: if Power or Air reaches zero, the crew flies home early.

Real NASA data. Each mission asks NASA’s DONKI space-weather database how many solar flares, or coronal mass ejections (CMEs), happened in the last 30 days. A busier real Sun means a higher storm chance. The game always says where its number came from: LIVE, hours ago, SAVED with its date, or PRACTICE MODE. It never presents saved data as live.

Scoring. At the end, Tar-Ra gives a score out of 100: survival 40, science 30, supplies 20, crew safety 10. She adds 1–3 stars, a rank from Trainee to Mission Commander, and one tip based on what went wrong.

Benefits

  • Hands-on learning: kids learn trade-offs by making them, not by reading about them. Every choice has a visible cost.
  • Real science: after each card, Tar-Ra shares a short fact based on NASA research. Topics include oxygen made on the Space Station, regolith as radiation shielding, ice in permanently shadowed craters, and fuel cells on Apollo.
  • Honest about data: kids see that scientists track space weather, and that data has a source and a date.
  • Short and replayable: a full mission takes about 10–15 minutes. “Play Again” skips the tutorial.
  • Two languages: English and Montenegrin, switched with one button on the main menu.

Intended impact

I want children to understand that living beyond Earth is a constant balancing act. Every breath, watt and layer of shielding has to be planned. I hope they leave curious about real missions like Artemis, and confident that careful thinking, not luck, keeps astronauts safe. The Montenegrin version brings NASA science to children who rarely get space-education games in their own language.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Engine and language: Godot 4.7.1 (GL Compatibility renderer) and GDScript.
    • Tar-Ra is my own drawing, later converted in some places to 256×256 pixel art.
    • The main menu background is hand-made.
    • The game background, the 16 card pictures, the icons and the UI frames are handdrawn.
  • Fonts: Pixelify Sans and Press Start 2P, both under the open SIL Open Font License.
  • Development help: Claude Code (an AI coding assistant), connected to Godot through the Godot MCP server.
  • Hardware: a standard Windows 11 PC.
  • Release: a single Windows exe.

How it’s creative

  • A guide with a story: Tar-Ra’s name links the game’s mentor to Earth itself (“Terra became Tar-Ra”), giving kids an emotional anchor to home.
  • Trade-offs as cards: every card has both sides, so there is never a “free” right answer. That is the core lesson of the challenge.
  • Real weather in the game: the real Sun’s activity this month changes how dangerous your mission is.
  • One visual style: a pixel-art look with a hologram shader on Tar-Ra.

Factors I considered

  • Age 7–12: short sentences, simple words, color-coded resources, one decision per day, and a practice card before the real mission.
  • Gentle failure: if the mission ends early, the crew “came home safe”. Tar-Ra frames it as learning, not losing.
  • Data honesty: clear labels, dated saved readings, and a practice fallback when offline. The game says plainly that card numbers are simplified.
  • Reliability and privacy: responses are cached for 6 hours to respect NASA’s rate limits. The public build uses NASA’s public demo key, so no personal key is shipped.
  • Balance: I simulated thousands of games and tuned the numbers until thoughtful players usually win and careless ones often don’t.
  • Fair storm experience: every mission brings a storm warning by day 5, so every player learns about shielding.
  • Readability: an arcade font with very clear digits for numbers, and a softer pixel font for reading.
  • Translation care: Montenegrin text avoids addressing the player as a boy or a girl, and I checked that special letters (č, ć, š, ž, đ) display correctly.
